transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I mean, I'm here because... it's just been a really strange few months, honestly. I work as a personal financial advisor, right? So I deal with a lot of people, a lot of networking, especially in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati. It's a tight-knit group, you know, you see the same faces at gallery openings, charity dinners, panel discussions, that sort of thing. But lately—and by lately, I mean for a while now, probably a few months—I've become absolutely convinced that certain individuals in these circles are... well, they're tracking me. Quietly, of course. Not like following me down the street, but tracking which clients I'm meeting with, who I'm talking to, what deals I might be advising on. 

And it's not just a feeling. They're sending me these... signals. Little messages. Like, I'll get an invitation to a very specific event right after I've had a confidential meeting with a client, and the theme of the event will perfectly mirror what we just discussed behind closed doors. Or I'll be at a panel discussion, and the topics the speakers choose to focus on—the exact phrasing they use—it's directed right at me. Even something as simple as the seating arrangements at these dinners. I'll notice who they purposely seat next to me, and it's always someone connected to a move I'm making, like they're trying to tell me they know. They know what I'm doing. 

And the thing is, I'm an educated guy, I have my bachelor's, I analyze data for a living. So a part of my brain says, "Okay, maybe it's just a coincidence. Cincinnati isn't that big, circles overlap." I tell myself that. I really do. I try to rationalize it. But then another invitation comes, or another person sits next to me with that knowing look, and I just... I can't let it go. It's too specific, too coordinated. It's like this elaborate puzzle they're laying out for me, and I can't stop trying to figure out what they want me to do with the information. So, yeah, that's... that's why I'm here. Because it's starting to really take up a lot of my mental space.
Have you ever heard voices or sounds that other people cannot hear, especially in relation to these perceived messages or signals?

No, no, it's not... I know what you're asking, and it's not like that at all. I don't hear whispers in the walls or, you know, imaginary voices when I'm alone in my apartment or anything. Everything I'm talking about is very grounded in the physical world, which is exactly why it's so hard for me to just brush it off. 

The signals I'm picking up on, they are entirely real things that anyone else in the room could hear or see. Like, if I'm at a charity gala—take the one they held last month over at the Taft Museum, for instance—I hear the string quartet playing, I hear the clinking of the champagne glasses, I hear the exact same ambient noise as the guy standing right next to me. The difference isn't that I'm hearing a secret sound they can't hear. The difference is in the actual, literal words people are choosing to say out loud when I'm in earshot. It's the subtext. 

So if two gallery directors are standing near the bar discussing a new exhibit on, I don't know, "hidden structures," they're saying those exact words out loud. Anyone walking by can hear them. But I'm the one who knows they chose that specific phrasing because I just advised a private client on restructuring their hidden assets two days prior. 

So, no, I've never heard a sound or a voice that someone else couldn't physically hear. My hearing is perfectly normal. It's just that other people don't realize the weight of what's being said out loud, you know? They just hear standard networking small talk, whereas I can see the puzzle pieces fitting together in real time. But as for literal voices in my head? No, definitely not. It's all real conversations, just... coordinated.
Have these beliefs about being tracked and receiving signals changed at all over the past few months?

Well, I should probably clarify the timeline on that first. I know I said "a few months" earlier, but if I really sit down and look at my planner—and I live by my planner, you know, you absolutely have to in my line of work, keeping track of every lunch, every call—it’s actually been going on for about two months. Pretty much exactly two months, give or take a few days. 

I can trace it back to this specific week. I was putting together a rather complex asset allocation strategy for a new client, someone very private, and then... bam. That weekend, the very first undeniable signal happened at a silent auction downtown. So for these past two months, this whole thing—the tracking of my client meetings, the specific wording people are using, the signals they're sending me—it hasn't really changed in *how* they do it, but it's just been so constant. Like this steady, relentless drumbeat for eight weeks straight. 

You know, at first, in week one or two of this, I thought, "Okay, maybe I'm just stressed, maybe it's just end-of-quarter fatigue making me read into things." I really tried to give it the benefit of the doubt. But then it kept happening. Week three, week four. Every single time I had a confidential meeting, someone would drop a perfectly tailored hint at a networking event a day or two later. 

So over these two months, the only thing that's really changed is my own realization that it's absolutely deliberate. The tracking itself hasn't escalated into anything dangerous, it hasn't changed its shape, it’s just... it's settled in. It's become this permanent fixture in my professional life. I've spent the better part of these two months trying to map it all out, looking at who was where, what they said, what deals I was working on at that exact moment. I even started keeping a separate notebook just to cross-reference the dates of my client meetings with the dates of the events where the signals happen. And when you look at two months of data like that, the correlation is just impossible to ignore. It’s just... it’s a lot of data to process when it’s been happening non-stop for two solid months, you know?
Have you ever considered the possibility that these signals might not be intended for you, or that there could be another explanation for the coincidences you're noticing?

Well, yes, absolutely. I mean, I try to do that all the time. Like I was saying when I first came in, I really do try to rationalize it. I sit down with my notebooks—because I'm an analytical guy, right? I analyze data for my clients, I look at market trends, I know how to separate random noise from an actual statistical pattern. So I'll sit there, usually late at night at my kitchen table, and I actively try to poke holes in my own theory. I’ll say to myself, "Okay, maybe that panel topic was planned six months ago. Maybe the seating chart at the charity dinner was just alphabetical, or based on who requested the vegetarian meal." I genuinely try to find the mundane, everyday explanation for it all. 

But then... I just can't let it go. I really can't. Because it's not just one coincidence, you know? It's the sheer volume of it. Like I mentioned, I’ve been convinced for a while now that these specific people—the ones running things in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati—are quietly tracking exactly which clients I meet with. And it’s those little signals they keep sending to let me know they're watching. The perfectly timed invitations, the hyper-specific panel topics, even who they purposely seat near me at these events. I tell myself, over and over, that it could just be a coincidence, but when you have dozens of coincidences lining up perfectly with your private, confidential schedule... mathematically, that stops being a coincidence. It becomes a coordinated effort. 

And I spend hours thinking about the logistics of it, trying to prove myself wrong. I’ll think, "Hey, maybe you're reading too much into this, maybe these signals aren't intended for you at all." But then I look at the timeline in my planner. If I meet with a client about a very niche tax shelter on a Tuesday, and on Thursday I get a VIP invitation to a gallery opening titled "Sheltered Assets"... I mean, how else am I supposed to interpret that? I try to walk away from it, I try to just do my job and ignore the networking scene, but the evidence just keeps piling up. It's exhausting, honestly, constantly trying to balance the logical, rational side of my brain with what is so obviously, undeniably happening right in front of me.
Have these beliefs about being tracked and receiving signals affected your relationships with friends, family, or colleagues?

Well, it's... it's definitely had an impact, yeah. I mean, it's hard to explain without getting into the weeds of how my daily routine has shifted, but... I don't know, things just feel different lately. Even putting the signals aside for a second, my day-to-day interactions have just sort of... flattened out, I guess you could say. 

At work, for instance, I'm still getting my core tasks done. If I have to draft a financial plan, I'll draft it. But I do it in pieces now. I used to be the guy who would bang out a comprehensive portfolio review in one sitting, completely energized by the strategy of it all. Now, I'll do a section, stop, stare at the screen for a while, maybe do another section later. I just don't have that same spark I used to have. The drive is gone. And the follow-ups—oh man, the client follow-ups. I used to be so proactive, calling people just to check in, but lately I'll just leave those tasks sitting on my desk for days. It's not even that I'm anxious about making the calls, it's just... I just don't feel the urge to do it. The motivation just isn't there.

And it bleeds over into my personal life, too. A lot, actually. My buddies have this regular pickup basketball game on Thursday nights, and there's a jazz club downtown I used to hit up on weekends. I used to love doing those things. But lately, I've just been skipping them. And the weirdest part is, I don't even feel bad about missing out. I don't feel much of anything about it, honestly. I just stay home. 

When my friends do text or call to ask where I've been or what's going on, I just give them these really short, one-word answers. "I'm fine," "Just busy," that kind of thing. Because honestly, the thought of trying to explain everything, or even just having a normal, casual conversation... it just feels like so much effort. More effort than it should be, you know? It's like the energy required to just talk to people has doubled, and my battery is constantly at ten percent. So, yeah, it's definitely affecting my relationships, but maybe not in the dramatic, confrontational way you might think. It's more like I'm just quietly fading into the background because I don't have the energy to participate anymore.
Have you stopped doing anything you normally enjoy because of these beliefs about being tracked?

Well, yes, especially when it comes to the parts of my career that I actually used to find really fun. I mean, I know people think being a financial advisor is just staring at spreadsheets all day, but the real enjoyment—at least for me, historically—was always the outward-facing stuff. The networking, the relationship building, being out there in the community. I used to absolutely love sitting on these public panels, you know, talking about market forecasts or tax strategies to a room full of local business owners. It was thrilling, honestly. It was how I built my reputation. 

But now... I just can't do it. I actively avoid some of those public panels now. I'll get an email asking me to moderate a discussion on, say, municipal bonds at the chamber of commerce, and I just have to decline. Because I know if I go, that's exactly where they're going to drop the next signal. I'll be sitting on the stage, and someone in the audience will ask a question that perfectly mirrors a private conversation I had in my office three days prior. I just don't want to subject myself to that feeling of being exposed, so I stay away.

And the ripple effect of that is... well, I’m still working, obviously, I haven't closed my doors, but my practice has gotten smaller. It’s noticeably shrinking. Between avoiding the events where I used to get my best leads, and just... well, like I was saying earlier about the follow-ups. I miss follow-ups all the time now. Before, it was maybe just because I felt drained, but it's also because every time I reach out to a client, every time I make a move or schedule a review, I feel like I'm just feeding more data into whatever system these people are using to track me. 

So I hold back. I really have trouble keeping up the same level of client contact I used to manage. I used to be the guy who remembered every client's birthday, their kids' college majors, and I'd call them up just to chat and check in on their portfolios. I thrived on that. Now, I keep the contact to the absolute bare minimum, usually just emails, because the more I interact with them, the more material I give the people watching me to use at the next event. So yeah, the enjoyable parts of the job, the socializing, the growth, the connection... I've had to just let a lot of that go to protect myself, and it's definitely taking a toll on the business.
Have you experienced significant anxiety or fear as a result of believing you are being tracked?

Anxiety? Fear? No, I... I wouldn't really use those words. I mean, it's a logical question, I get why you'd ask that. A lot of people, if they realized a whole network of local finance and arts people were coordinating to monitor their private client meetings, they’d probably be terrified. They’d be looking over their shoulder, having panic attacks, that kind of thing. But for me... it’s not really like that. Like I said, I'm an analytical guy. I look at it as a data problem. 

So I don't sit in my apartment shaking or sweating. It’s more just... well, it goes back to what I was telling you about my energy levels. It’s just this massive, exhausting administrative burden. Think about it like an audit. If you’re a financial advisor and you know a regulatory body is auditing your practice, you aren't necessarily hiding under your desk in fear, right? But you are completely drained by the constant need to double-check every single piece of paperwork, every email, every interaction. That’s exactly how this feels. I’m not scared of them. I’m just so tired of having to factor their surveillance into my daily logistics. 

Like, just the other week, I was planning to go grab lunch at this deli I like downtown. But then I realized the route would take me right past the venue where the chamber of commerce was hosting that municipal bond panel I had to decline. I didn't feel a spike of fear, I didn't have a racing heart or anything. I just thought, "Ugh, I really don't want to deal with the hassle of running into one of them and having them drop another perfectly timed hint about my Tuesday morning meeting." So I just didn't go. I stayed in my office and ate a stale granola bar I had in my desk. 

It’s not fear, it’s just... I don't know, I just feel kind of numb to it at this point. I don't even have the emotional bandwidth to be scared. It just feels like a giant, endless logistical puzzle that I’m forced to navigate every single day, and it just depletes whatever small amount of motivation I have left. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm anxious. Just profoundly, deeply exhausted by the whole production of it.

I mean, I do try to rationalize it. I really do. I'll sit in my office after everyone goes home, just looking at the wall, and I tell myself, "Look, maybe it could just be coincidence." Because for a while now, I’ve been absolutely convinced that certain people—specifically this tight-knit, overlapping group in the arts and finance circles right here in Cincinnati—are quietly tracking exactly which clients I meet with. Like, how could a gallery owner just happen to seat me next to a municipal bond specialist two days after I drafted a municipal bond strategy for a new client? You see what I mean? It's too precise. It's too coordinated. So even when I actively sit down, take a deep breath, and tell myself that it could just be a random coincidence, I just... I can’t really let it go. I try to brush it off, I try to accept that maybe it's just a fluke, but my mind just keeps snagging on the details because the pattern is just so undeniably there.

I've been playing with the exact same group of guys—mostly other young professionals, a couple of lawyers, a dentist—since I moved here after I got my degree. We had a really good thing going, usually a solid five-on-five, and it was a great way to burn off steam. But lately... I just don't go. I'll look at my gym bag sitting right there by the door, and I just think about the sheer mechanics of it—putting on the shoes, driving over there, running up and down the court—and I just skip it. And the weirdest part is, I do it without much feeling about it at all. I don't feel sad or frustrated that I'm missing out. I just feel kind of flat. 

And it's the exact same thing with my weekends. There's this jazz club over in the arts district—really great acoustic setup, local musicians, mostly brass, which I love. I used to be a regular there. I'd go on a Friday night, grab a small table in the back, order a drink, and just soak in the music. It was my favorite way to decompress after staring at portfolios all week. Now? I just let those jazz nights completely pass me by. I'll even see an email newsletter about a band I actually really like playing, and I just can't muster the energy to care or get off the couch.

And I find myself just giving these incredibly short answers. "Just busy." "Tired." "Working." Because honestly, just the thought of having a full conversation, of actually explaining anything or even just engaging in normal back-and-forth banter... it just feels like so much effort. Way more effort than it ever should be. It’s like just forming the sentences and pushing the words out of my mouth is this massive physical chore.
